set.detail:
The Mamertines ('sons of Mars') were Campanian mercenaries of Agathocles who seized Messana around 288, killed or expelled its men and took their wives and property. For two decades they raided eastern Sicily until Hiero, the new general of Syracuse, defeated them at the Longanus (c. 269 or 265) and besieged the city. One faction then admitted a Carthaginian garrison under Hanno; another appealed to Rome, citing kinship as Italians. Polybius (1.10-11) says the Senate could not decide, because Rome had just executed the Campanian legion that had seized Rhegium in exactly the same way (270), but feared that Carthage, already master of Africa, much of Spain, Sardinia and the western half of Sicily, would control the Straits and encircle Italy. The consuls, Appius Claudius Caudex above all, took the question to the people, holding out the prospect of booty, and the assembly voted to receive the Mamertines into alliance. The military tribune Gaius Claudius crossed the Straits; the Mamertines tricked or pushed Hanno out of the citadel, and Carthage crucified him for cowardice. Carthage and Hiero then allied and besieged Messana together, which turned a police action into war with both Sicilian powers.

The sources are thin and partisan. Polybius used Fabius Pictor, who blamed the war on Carthaginian aggression, and Philinus of Agrigentum, who claimed that Rome broke a treaty barring it from Sicily. Polybius denies that such a treaty existed (3.26), but many modern scholars accept a version of it, perhaps a misreading of the treaty of 306. Dio and Zonaras preserve a more elaborate annalistic narrative with negotiations in Messana. The decision to cross has become the classic test case for theories of Roman imperialism: Mommsen saw defensive necessity, Harris (1979) a society geared to war, gloria and plunder, Hoyos (1998) an 'unplanned war' that both powers expected to be short, and Eckstein (2006) normal behaviour in a multipolar anarchy. The role of the people, unusual in Polybius' account, is also debated: either the Senate really was split, or the historian (via Fabius) shifted responsibility for a fateful decision away from the governing class.

scholarship: Rich, in Rich and Shipley (eds.), War and Society in the Roman World (1993)

set.detail:
Messana was under siege by Hiero from the south-west and a Carthaginian army under another Hanno (son of Hannibal) from the north, with a Carthaginian fleet watching the Straits from Cape Pelorias. Appius Claudius Caudex, consul 264 with two legions and allies, perhaps 16,000 to 20,000 men, could not force the crossing by day. According to Polybius he crossed by night from Rhegium and entered Messana. He then sent envoys to both besiegers demanding that they lift the siege; when they refused, he attacked Hiero first, and after a hard fight drove the Syracusans back to their camp. Hiero, suspecting that the Carthaginians had betrayed him, withdrew to Syracuse that night. Appius then attacked the Carthaginian camp, defeated Hanno's forces and raided up to the walls of Syracuse.

The later tradition, preserved by Zonaras (from Dio) and partly by Frontinus, adds colour: a first attempt to cross ended in disaster when storms and the Carthaginian ships wrecked the Roman transports; Hanno returned the captured ships, warning that the Romans would not even wash their hands in the sea without Carthaginian permission; the Romans then crossed on rafts and triremes borrowed from Tarentum, Locri, Velia and Neapolis. Philinus, Polybius tells us, claimed instead that Appius was beaten by both enemies, and Polybius himself admits he cannot reconcile his sources (1.15). Modern accounts (Lazenby, Hoyos) accept the substance of Roman success but doubt that Appius won two separate battles on successive days; the Carthaginians may simply have pulled back to their fortresses at the end of the season.

The consequences were large. Hiero, isolated, made peace with Rome in 263 when the two consuls of that year marched on Syracuse with four legions. Messana remained a Roman base for the whole war and the start of Rome's Sicilian presence. Appius took no triumph, perhaps a sign that the victory was less complete than the Fabian tradition claimed, while his successor Valerius took the cognomen Messalla and triumphed.

In 263 both consuls, Manius Valerius Maximus and Manius Otacilius Crassus, crossed to Sicily with four legions, the full levy of the year. Polybius reports that 67 Sicilian towns, Greek and Sicel, went over to Rome and that the consuls advanced on Syracuse itself. Hiero, already ruling for nearly twenty years and realising that Carthage could not protect him, negotiated. He returned his prisoners without ransom, paid 100 talents (Diodorus has 150,000 drachmas, roughly 25 talents, and a later passage 100 talents to be paid over 15 years), and became Rome's friend and ally, keeping Syracuse and a strip of south-eastern Sicily, about 50 miles deep, including Leontini, Megara, Akrai, Helorus, Netum and Tauromenium. The treaty was renewed for life in 248.

The alliance transformed the war. Hiero's grain, siege technology (supplied at Agrigentum, Camarina and Lipara) and ships kept Roman armies supplied throughout, and Polybius praises his steady loyalty. Rome no longer needed to fight a war on two fronts and could concentrate on the Carthaginian west. For Hiero it secured his kingdom; he survived to 215, enriched by the Sicilian grain trade, gave Rome help again after Trasimene (a golden Victory weighing 320 pounds, grain and archers) and was the principal Greek benefactor of Rhodes after its earthquake. His tax law, the lex Hieronica, was later adopted by Rome for the province of Sicily.

The consul Valerius took the cognomen Messalla from Messana. From Catana he brought back a sundial, which was set up on a column by the Rostra; Pliny, following Varro, notes that it was calibrated for a latitude four degrees to the south and that the Romans used it for 99 years until Quintus Marcius Philippus installed one adjusted for Rome in 164. Valerius also displayed a painting of his victory over Hiero and the Carthaginians on the side wall of the Curia Hostilia, the first historical painting known at Rome. Modern scholars stress that by 263 Rome's aims had already grown beyond Messana: the scale of the army sent shows a decision to drive Carthage out of eastern Sicily at least.

scholarship: Serrati, Sicily in the Roman Republic (2000)

set.detail:
Carthage responded to the loss of eastern Sicily by concentrating a mercenary army, including Ligurians, Celts and many Iberians, at Agrigentum, the second Greek city of the island and its western base for the land war. In 262 both consuls, Lucius Postumius Megellus and Quintus Mamilius Vitulus, laid siege with four legions. They built two fortified camps joined by double lines of ditches, one against the city and one against relief, and drew supplies through Herbessus with Hiero's help. The garrison commander, Hannibal son of Gisco, held about 50,000 people in the city; after five months he was starving.

Carthage sent Hanno with a relief army that Polybius puts at 50,000 foot, 6,000 cavalry and 60 elephants. Hanno took Herbessus and cut the Roman supply line, so that the besiegers too suffered famine and disease. After two months of stalemate Hanno offered battle. The Romans won: Hanno's Numidian cavalry first drew the Roman horse forward, but the Roman infantry broke the mercenaries in front, the elephants panicked and fled through the rear lines. That night Hannibal and the garrison slipped out through the Roman lines, filling the ditches with baskets of straw. The Romans entered Agrigentum the next day, plundered it and sold 25,000 inhabitants into slavery.

Polybius (1.20) says that the capture of Agrigentum changed Roman war aims: the Senate now hoped to expel Carthage from Sicily entirely. But it also exposed the limits of a land strategy. Many inland towns came over to Rome, while the coastal cities feared the Carthaginian fleet and stayed loyal; Carthaginian ships raided Italy at will. Hence the decision of 261 to build a fleet. Diodorus' version (23.8-9), from Philinus, gives the Roman losses in the siege as 30,000 foot and 540 cavalry and blames Roman cruelty for driving the Sicilians back to Carthage. The sale of the population, the first enslavement of an entire Greek city by Rome, was a grim precedent, and Agrigentum, rebuilt with new settlers, changed hands twice more before 210.

scholarship: Hoyos, A Companion to the Punic Wars (2011)

set.detail:
Polybius (1.20-21) tells the story that became the founding myth of the Roman navy. Rome had never owned quinqueremes, and its shipwrights had no model; then a Carthaginian quinquereme that ran aground while attacking the Roman crossing in 264 was captured and copied. The Romans built 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes in sixty days from the felling of the timber, while crews practised rowing on benches set up on land. Pliny echoes the speed; Florus says the fleet seemed to grow from the trees by divine intervention.

Modern scholarship qualifies the legend. Rome had naval officers (duoviri navales, from 311) and allied ships from Tarentum, Neapolis, Locri and Velia (the socii navales), and the Greek cities of southern Italy had long traditions of shipbuilding and naval architecture, so expertise was not lacking. What Rome lacked was the quinquereme, the 'five' with probably three banks of oars and two or three rowers to some oars, which required a different construction and a crew of 300 rowers and 120 marines. The Marsala Punic shipwreck, excavated by Honor Frost in the 1970s, revealed letters painted on timbers as assembly marks, which supports the possibility of rapid prefabricated construction; the Egadi rams recovered off Levanzo since 2004 show the scale of the warships, with rams of about 100 to 170 kilograms.

The 120 ships needed about 30,000 rowers and 12,000 marines, perhaps a quarter of all Roman and allied men of military age, drawn especially from the proletarii and allied coastal towns. The building programme marks the moment Rome became a naval power, a decision driven by the stalemate after Agrigentum. The first squadron of 17 ships under Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio was trapped at Lipara, but within months the corvus (a boarding bridge, Polybius' 'raven') allowed Duilius to win at Mylae. Rome would build some 1,000 warships in the course of the war and lose perhaps 600 to 700 of them, mostly to storms, at a human cost of well over 100,000 men.

scholarship: Tusa and Royal, The landscape of the naval battle at the Egadi Islands, JRA 25 (2012)

set.detail:
In 260 the consul Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio had lost the first 17 Roman ships at Lipara, earning the nickname Asina ('she-ass'). His colleague Gaius Duilius, a new man who had been commanding the land army, took over the fleet of perhaps 103 ships. On the advice of an unknown engineer the Romans had fitted their ships with the corvus: a gangway 1.2 metres wide and 11 metres long, mounted on a pole in the bow, which could be swung round and dropped by pulley so that its iron spike pierced the enemy deck, letting marines board. Polybius' detailed description (1.22) is the only one; no remains have been found.

The Carthaginian fleet of 130 ships under Hannibal son of Gisco, the defender of Agrigentum, sailed from Panormus to meet the Romans off Mylae on the north coast of Sicily, contemptuous of Roman seamanship and in no battle order. The first thirty ships, including Hannibal's seven, the flagship once Pyrrhus', attacked head on and were all grappled and taken; Hannibal escaped in a small boat. The rest tried to attack from the sides and stern but the corvi swung round to meet them and they fled after losing 50 ships in all (Polybius gives 30 to 50; the Columna Rostrata claims 31 taken, 13 sunk, 3,000 or 7,000 prisoners).

Duilius celebrated Rome's first naval triumph and received lifelong honours: a torch and a flute-player escorting him home from dinner. A column decorated with rams stood in the Forum; its inscription, restored in the reign of Claudius in archaising Latin, survives in part (CIL I2 25) and lists the booty, including 3,600 pounds of gold and over 100,000 pounds of silver. Hannibal was recalled and, Polybius says, crucified by his own troops a few years later in Sardinia. Modern debate concerns the corvus itself, whose weight probably made ships unstable in rough seas and may have contributed to the later storm disasters (Thiel), and the reliability of the inscription's figures. Strategically, Mylae proved that Rome could fight Carthage at sea and opened the way to Corsica, Sardinia and eventually Africa.

scholarship: Thiel, A History of Roman Sea-Power before the Second Punic War (1954)
Wallinga, The Boarding-Bridge of the Romans (1956)

set.detail:
In summer 256 Rome launched the invasion of Africa. The consuls Lucius Manlius Vulso Longus and Marcus Atilius Regulus assembled 330 warships at Messana, embarked picked troops at Phintias, and sailed along the south coast of Sicily. Polybius (1.25-28) counts about 140,000 men on board (roughly 300 rowers and 120 marines a ship); the Carthaginian fleet under Hamilcar and Hanno, 350 ships with some 150,000 men, waited off Heraclea Minoa. Ecnomus, a hill near modern Licata, gave the battle its name; it may have been the largest naval battle in history by the number of combatants.

The Roman fleet sailed in a triangle: the consuls' two flagships, sexiremes, at the apex leading the first and second squadrons in echelon, the third squadron towing horse transports across the base, and the fourth (the triarii) in a line behind. The Carthaginians spread in a long line from the shore, planning to envelop. Their centre deliberately fell back before the Roman first and second squadrons, drawing them away, while Hanno's right wing attacked the rear and the Carthaginian left fell on the third squadron pinned against the shore. The battle split into three separate fights. Polybius' battle narrative has been argued over at length because the formation seems unwieldy, but it made sense as a defensive arrangement protecting the transports.

The Carthaginian centre eventually fled from the consuls, who then turned to rescue the third and fourth squadrons; the corvus again prevented the Carthaginians from exploiting their skill, and they were forced against the shore. The Romans lost 24 ships sunk; the Carthaginians had over 30 sunk and 64 captured with their crews. The victory opened the way to Africa: after refitting the Romans landed at Aspis on the Cape Bon peninsula. Tarn and Thiel doubted Polybius' numbers, suggesting rather 230 to 250 Roman ships, but most recent historians accept them as broadly right. The battle also showed the strategic logic of the new navy: a fleet as the means of carrying a land war to the enemy's home.

scholarship: Tarn, The Fleets of the First Punic War, JHS 27 (1907)
Tipps, The Battle of Ecnomus, Historia 34 (1985)

set.detail:
After Adys, Regulus took Tunes and wintered within sight of Carthage. Refugees, Numidian raids and food shortages had broken Carthaginian morale, but Regulus' terms (evacuation of Sicily and Sardinia, release of Roman prisoners without ransom, payment of Roman war costs, a tribute, and restrictions on the Carthaginian navy) were so harsh that the Carthaginians preferred to fight. Among the Greek mercenaries recruited that winter was a Spartan, Xanthippus, who criticised the generals for fighting in hills where their elephants and cavalry, their real strengths, were useless. Polybius (1.32-34) says he was given effective command.

In spring 255 Xanthippus led out 12,000 infantry, 4,000 cavalry and nearly 100 elephants onto open ground, probably in the Bagradas valley. Regulus, with about 15,000 foot and 500 horse, deepened his infantry formation to resist the elephants. The elephants in front of the Carthaginian line trampled the Roman centre; the Roman left beat the mercenaries opposite and pursued them to the camp, but the Carthaginian cavalry routed the few Roman horse and then took the legions in flank and rear. Only about 2,000 Romans on the left escaped to Aspis; Regulus and 500 men were captured. The Carthaginians lost about 800 mercenaries.

Polybius moralises at length: the fall of Regulus, who had refused moderation, shows the instability of fortune, and the victory of Xanthippus shows how one intelligent man can transform a cause. Xanthippus left soon after, either because Carthaginian jealousy was rising or, in a later story, to escape assassination at sea. The defeat ended the African invasion. A relief fleet of 350 ships won off Cape Hermaeum and picked up the survivors, only to be wrecked off Camarina on the way home. The Regulus legend (embassy to Rome, advice against peace, return to death by torture in Carthage) belongs to later Roman tradition and is doubted by most historians, though his death in captivity is plausible. Modern assessments stress Regulus' tactical misjudgment in fighting on open ground with weak cavalry, a lesson Rome learned again at the Trebia and Cannae.

The relief fleet sent in 255 under the consuls Servius Fulvius Paetinus Nobilior and Marcus Aemilius Paullus had won a crushing victory over a Carthaginian fleet of 200 off Cape Hermaeum, taking 114 ships with their crews. Having embarked the survivors of Regulus' army at Aspis, the fleet of some 364 ships returned towards Sicily in July. Polybius (1.37) says that the captains warned the consuls not to sail along the south coast of Sicily, which was harbourless and exposed to the south-westerly gales of the season between the rising of Orion and of Sirius, but the consuls wanted to impress the coastal towns. Off Camarina a storm drove the fleet onto the rocks: only 80 ships survived, and the shore from Camarina to Cape Pachynus was strewn with wreckage and bodies.

If the warships carried their normal crews, losses could have reached 100,000 men, the worst maritime disaster in ancient history; even allowing for undermanned ships and prize crews, tens of thousands drowned. Many of the dead were rowers drawn from the poorer citizens and the allied coastal communities. Polybius blames Roman stubbornness and the habit of relying on force in every circumstance, which worked on land but not against the sea, and observes that the Romans often failed for this reason. Modern writers add the weight of the corvus on the prow, which may have made the ships unseaworthy in heavy weather.

Despite the loss, the consuls triumphed in 254 for the victory at Hermaeum, and Rome immediately built 220 new ships in three months, which took Panormus in 254. A second disaster off Cape Palinurus in 253, when 150 ships were lost returning from an African raid, and the loss of Junius Pullus' convoy off Pachynus in 249 completed a record of storm losses that dwarfed Roman battle losses. The census figures, falling from 297,797 in 252 to 241,212 in 247, register the cost. The Camarina disaster marks the moment when Rome learned, slowly, the seamanship that its victories at sea had concealed.

scholarship: Thiel, A History of Roman Sea-Power before the Second Punic War (1954)

set.detail:
By 251 Rome had built back its fleets but, after the Palinurus disaster, avoided the sea, and Hasdrubal son of Hanno brought a large Carthaginian army with elephants (Polybius: 140; others 100 to 142) to western Sicily, confident because the Romans had feared to face elephants since Tunes. In late summer 250, when the consul Gaius Furius Pacilus had left with half the army, Hasdrubal advanced from Lilybaeum to the territory of Panormus to ravage its crops at harvest. The proconsul Lucius Caecilius Metellus kept his men inside the city walls, provoking Hasdrubal to cross the river Oreto in front of the city.

Metellus had dug a trench near the walls and stationed light infantry in front of it with ample supplies of javelins, ordering them to shower the elephants and, when pressed, to retreat into the ditch. Polybius (1.40) describes how the elephants, maddened by the missiles, turned back through their own lines; Metellus then sallied from a side gate with his main force against the disordered Carthaginian flank. The Carthaginians fled, many drowning or being cut down at the sea, where their fleet could not take them off. Metellus captured ten elephants with their mahouts in the battle and rounded up the rest later; tradition gives up to 120.

The victory restored Roman confidence on land and won Metellus enormous prestige: he shipped the elephants across the Straits on rafts made of empty jars and paraded them in his triumph, and the elephant became an emblem of the Caecilii Metelli on coins for generations. He later became pontifex maximus and, in 241, saved the Palladium from the burning temple of Vesta, losing his sight. Hasdrubal was executed at Carthage. Strategically, the battle encouraged Rome to attempt a decisive blow against Lilybaeum, the last major Carthaginian base besides Drepana, by land and sea. It is also one of the earliest examples of a Roman commander using field works and missile troops to neutralise elephants, a problem Scipio would solve differently at Zama.

scholarship: Scullard, The Elephant in the Greek and Roman World (1974)

set.detail:
Lilybaeum (modern Marsala), founded by the Carthaginians after the destruction of Motya in 397, stood on a promontory at the western tip of Sicily, protected by shoals, a deep ditch and walls, with a harbour reachable only by pilots who knew the channel. In 250, after Panormus, both consuls, Gaius Atilius Regulus Serranus and Lucius Manlius Vulso Longus, with four legions and 200 ships, attacked it by land and sea. The commander Himilco had 10,000 mercenaries. The Romans pushed rams and towers against the seaward towers and brought down six of them, but Himilco countermined and built an inner wall.

Polybius' account (1.41-55) is the most detailed narrative of a siege in his first book. Carthage sent 10,000 reinforcements under Hannibal son of Hamilcar, who ran the fleet into the harbour in a favourable wind while the Roman ships, fearing to be swept into the harbour, looked on. Hannibal the Rhodian ran the blockade repeatedly. A plot of mercenary officers to betray the city was foiled by the Achaean Alexon. A violent wind later allowed a sortie that burned the Roman siege works. Rome then settled for a blockade, which the disaster at Drepana in 249 and the loss of Junius Pullus' convoy turned into a loose investment by land only.

The siege lasted nine years, until the treaty of 241, with the garrison never taken. Its history illustrates the fundamental difficulty of the First Punic War: Rome, having won the open field and much of the sea, could not take fortified ports that Carthage supplied by sea. The decision to abandon assault for blockade, and the resources tied down at Lilybaeum and Drepana, kept Roman citizens and allies in the field for a decade, and the island's western tip became the hinge of the final campaign of 242-241, when Lutatius' fleet cut the sea lanes. After the war Lilybaeum became the seat of the second quaestor in the province of Sicily; excavations have uncovered its Punic walls, ditch and the Marsala Punic warship.

In 249 the consul Publius Claudius Pulcher, son of Appius Claudius Caecus, took over the fleet at Lilybaeum, reinforced it with 10,000 new rowers and planned a surprise night attack on the Carthaginian fleet of the admiral Adherbal in the harbour of Drepana, 25 kilometres to the north. Polybius (1.49-51) says the fleet of 123 ships left at midnight and arrived at dawn, but the line stretched out and Adherbal, seeing the leading ships entering the harbour, led his fleet out by the other side of the island-studded entrance and formed up in open water.

Claudius, at the rear, ordered his leading ships to reverse out of the harbour; they collided with those still coming in and were caught in a confused line along the shore, prows towards the enemy and sterns to the land. The Carthaginians, with better ships and more skilled crews, had room to manoeuvre, ram and retreat; the Romans had no room to back water. The Roman losses were 93 ships captured, with most crews; Claudius escaped with about 30. Adherbal lost no ships. It was Carthage's only major naval victory of the war.

The Roman tradition blamed sacrilege. Before the battle the sacred chickens, consulted for the auspices, refused to eat; Claudius threw them into the sea, saying 'let them drink, since they will not eat'. Cicero, Livy's epitomator, Suetonius and Valerius Maximus repeat the story. Recalled to Rome, Claudius was told to appoint a dictator and named his freedman clerk Marcus Claudius Glicia, who was forced to resign. Claudius was tried for perduellio, escaped condemnation when a storm interrupted the assembly, but was fined 120,000 asses on a lesser charge and died soon afterwards. His sister's remark in 246 suggests the defeat remained a byword. Modern accounts see a plan that was sound in principle but botched in execution by poor coordination and by the inexperience of the new rowers, and note that the same year saw the loss of Pullus' convoy. Rome built no new fleet for six years.

scholarship: Rawson, Religion and Politics in the Late Second Century, Phoenix (1974)

set.detail:
By 243 Rome's treasury could no longer fund a fleet, and leading citizens lent money individually or in syndicates of two or three to build 200 quinqueremes on the model of the captured ship of Hannibal the Rhodian, to be repaid if the war was won. In summer 242 the consul Gaius Lutatius Catulus took the fleet to Sicily, seized the harbour of Drepana and the anchorages near Lilybaeum, and spent the winter training his crews intensively. Carthage, which had laid up most of its fleet to save money, hastily manned about 250 ships under Hanno, loaded them with grain and supplies for Hamilcar's army on Eryx, and sent them to Hiera (Marettimo) in the Aegates islands, planning to run in, unload, embark Hamilcar's veterans as marines and then fight.

On the day conventionally given as 10 March 241 (a Roman calendar date, uncertain in Julian terms), with a strong westerly wind behind the Carthaginians, Lutatius, still lame from his wound, decided to fight in rough seas rather than let the convoy reach Sicily. The heavily laden Carthaginian ships with raw crews were outfought by the lighter, well-drilled Roman ships, which no longer used the corvus. Polybius (1.60-61) says 50 Carthaginian ships were sunk and 70 captured with their crews (later sources give 10,000 prisoners); the rest escaped when the wind changed. Hanno was crucified on his return.

Since 2004 the Soprintendenza del Mare of Sicily and the RPM Nautical Foundation have recovered more than twenty bronze warship rams and dozens of helmets from the seabed west of Levanzo, the only ancient naval battlefield identified archaeologically. Some rams carry Latin inscriptions naming quaestors who approved the castings; others carry Punic inscriptions, and several appear to be Roman-made rams on captured Carthaginian ships. The battle ended the war: Carthage, unable to supply Sicily, authorised Hamilcar to negotiate, and the treaty of Lutatius followed. Victory came from Roman staying power and private patriotism, but also from a professionalism at sea that Rome had learned at enormous cost.

scholarship: Tusa and Royal, The landscape of the naval battle at the Egadi Islands, JRA 25 (2012)
Prag, Bronze rostra from the site of the battle of the Aegates Islands, JRA 27 (2014)

set.detail:
After the Aegates, Hamilcar Barca, authorised by Carthage, negotiated with Lutatius Catulus. Polybius (1.62) gives the preliminary terms: Carthage was to evacuate all of Sicily, not make war on Hiero or his allies, return all Roman prisoners without ransom and pay 2,200 Euboean talents over twenty years. The Roman people rejected these and sent ten commissioners, who sharpened them: the indemnity rose to 3,200 talents, 1,000 payable immediately and the rest over ten years, and Carthage had to give up the islands between Sicily and Italy (the Aegates and Lipari). Each side undertook not to attack the other's allies, recruit troops or raise money in the other's territory, or make alliances with the other's allies. Hamilcar refused to hand over his men's arms and marched them down from Eryx with honour.

Polybius quotes later versions of the treaty (3.27) and we know that in 237, when Carthage prepared to reconquer Sardinia, Rome added a further 1,200 talents and the cession of Sardinia, a breach of the spirit of 241 that Polybius regarded as the real cause of the Second Punic War. The treaty made western Sicily the first Roman territory outside Italy. For the next fourteen years it was administered by the quaestors at Lilybaeum and visiting magistrates until praetors were sent in 227. The Greek cities of the west, such as Segesta and Halicyae, became free and immune; others paid a tithe on grain.

The indemnity, about 82,000 kilograms of silver, was the largest yet imposed in the western Mediterranean and contributed directly to the Mercenary War, since Carthage could not pay its troops. Modern scholars (Hoyos, Lazenby) emphasise that the terms were moderate compared with what Rome would impose in 201: Carthage kept its fleet, its African territory and Spain, and could recover. The Roman people's insistence on harsher terms than its general negotiated, a recurrent pattern, foreshadows the Senate's later treatment of Mancinus and Pompeius in Spain. The peace allowed Rome to close the doors of Janus in 235 for the first time since Numa.

Sardinia had been Carthaginian since the late sixth century, a source of grain and a naval base. During the Mercenary War its mercenary garrison revolted, crucified its commander Bostar and killed Carthaginian residents; the native Sardinians then drove the mercenaries out. The mercenaries fled to Italy and, in 240-239, invited Rome to take the island. At first Rome refused, keeping to the treaty and helping Carthage. But in 238/7, after the Mercenary War ended and Carthage prepared an expedition to recover Sardinia, Rome changed course: it declared that Carthage's preparations were aimed at Rome, voted war, and forced Carthage, exhausted and in no position to fight, to renounce Sardinia and pay an extra 1,200 talents.

Polybius condemns this (3.10, 3.28): it was against all justice, without reasonable pretext, and the anger it caused, along with Hamilcar's resentment, was the second of the three causes of the Hannibalic war. The Roman annalistic tradition tried to justify it, claiming that Carthage had mistreated Roman traders or that the island had been ceded in 241. Modern historians generally accept Polybius' judgment, though some (Hoyos) see a defensive motive: a revived Carthaginian navy in Sardinia would have threatened Italy's west coast. Rome also took Corsica, which Carthage had controlled or influenced.

Securing the islands took years. The consul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus occupied Sardinia in 238; campaigns against Sardinians and Corsicans followed in 235, 234, 233, 232 and 231 (with several triumphs), and the island remained restless until Gracchus' son crushed a major rising in 177-176. In 227 Sardinia and Corsica were made into a single province under a praetor. The seizure shows a new Roman readiness to exploit weakness in a former enemy, and the Barcid answer, the build-up of a Carthaginian empire in Spain from 237, followed directly.

scholarship: Dyson and Rowland, Archaeology and History in Sardinia (2007)

set.detail:
After the Mercenary War Hamilcar Barca, whose political base rested on the army and on the popular assembly at Carthage, was given command in Spain. In 237 he crossed to Gades with his army and his son-in-law Hasdrubal. Polybius (3.11), citing Hannibal's own words to Antiochus III, tells how before sailing Hamilcar took the nine-year-old Hannibal to the altar during a sacrifice and made him swear never to be a friend of Rome. Polybius makes Hamilcar's anger over Sicily and Sardinia the first cause of the Second Punic War.

For nine years Hamilcar fought and negotiated his way up the Baetis (Guadalquivir) valley and into the south-east, defeating the Turdetani and the Celtic leaders Istolatius and Indortes, the latter of whom he blinded and crucified while releasing 10,000 prisoners. He founded a base at Akra Leuke (perhaps Alicante or near it) and exploited the silver of the Sierra Morena and around Castulo. Coins struck in Spain under the Barcids, with portrait heads sometimes read as Hamilcar and Hannibal in the guise of Melqart, show the dynasty's semi-royal style. Fabius Pictor and the Roman tradition portrayed the Spanish venture as a private Barcid empire, built without Carthage's consent; Polybius (3.8) rejects this, pointing out that the Carthaginian government confirmed Hasdrubal and then Hannibal in command.

Hamilcar's Spanish dominion repaired the losses of Sicily and Sardinia: Spanish silver paid the remaining indemnity to Rome, and Spanish manpower provided the core of the army that crossed the Alps. Dio and Zonaras record a Roman embassy in 231 that asked Hamilcar what he was doing; he replied that he was fighting to pay off Carthage's debts to Rome. He died in 229 or 228 besieging Helice, drowning while covering the retreat of his sons. Modern scholars debate whether the Barcids planned a war of revenge from the start (Polybius' view) or whether Spain was simply the best available source of wealth and power for a Carthage shut out of the islands (Hoyos, Lancel).

The Ardiaean kingdom of Agron and, after his death in 231, his widow Teuta, regent for the boy Pinnes, had become the leading power on the eastern Adriatic, raiding Epirus, sacking Phoenice in 230 and preying on Italian traders. When the Roman envoys Gaius and Lucius Coruncanius complained, Teuta replied that it was not the custom of Illyrian kings to stop their subjects from profiting at sea; one envoy was murdered on the way home. In 229 the Illyrians besieged Corcyra, Epidamnus and Issa and, after beating the Achaean and Aetolian fleets off Paxos, took Corcyra and left Demetrius of Pharos in command.

Rome responded with both consuls. Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus sailed with 200 ships to Corcyra, where Demetrius, in secret contact with Rome, handed over the island and his garrison; Corcyra entered Roman fides. Lucius Postumius Albinus crossed from Brundisium with 20,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry to Apollonia. The Romans relieved Epidamnus, accepted the surrender of the Parthini and Atintani, and relieved Issa; Teuta fled to Rhizon. In spring 228 she made peace: she paid tribute, gave up all of Illyria except a few places, and undertook not to sail beyond Lissus with more than two unarmed lembi. Demetrius received territories as a Roman friend.

Polybius (2.2-12) calls this the first Roman crossing in arms to Illyria and the first Roman official contact with Greece: envoys went to the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues, and then to Corinth and Athens, explaining the reasons for the war; Corinth admitted Romans to the Isthmian Games. Rome created no province, only a loose protectorate of free communities (Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus, Issa, the Parthini, Atintani), and withdrew its forces, a pattern of eastern policy that persisted until 148. Holleaux saw the war as a reluctant response to the needs of Italian traders, Harris and Derow as part of a broader expansionism. The protectorate brought Rome into conflict with Macedon, whose interests in Illyria it touched, and ten years later with Demetrius himself.

scholarship: Holleaux, Rome, la Grèce et les monarchies hellénistiques (1921)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)

set.detail:
Until 227 Rome had governed western Sicily and Sardinia-Corsica without permanent magistrates: the quaestors stationed at Lilybaeum and possibly Ostia managed the fleet and revenues, and consuls or praetors campaigned when needed. In 227 the number of praetors was raised from two to four, and the first two praetors with provincial responsibilities were sent out: Gaius Flaminius to Sicily and Marcus Valerius Laevinus to Sardinia. Solinus and the Digest (Pomponius) give the date; Livy's Periochae (20) mention the increase. The word provincia, originally a sphere of command, now acquired its territorial sense.

The new praetors had imperium and courts, military command over garrisons, and responsibility for revenue. Western Sicily paid the tithe (decuma) on grain, collected by contractors under rules later codified in the lex Hieronica, which Rome took over from Hiero's kingdom when it absorbed Syracuse in 211; a few cities were free and immune and others, such as Messana and Tauromenium, had treaties. Sardinia paid a fixed tribute (stipendium) and grain. Gaius Flaminius seems to have been remembered well by the Sicilians: in 196 they sent his son a gift of grain when he was aedile.

The reform marks the birth of the Roman provincial system and the beginning of the cursus of praetorian commands. It also set a pattern of slow, incremental institution building: the praetorship was increased again to six in 197 for the two Spains, Macedonia and Africa received governors in 146, and the permanent extortion court of 149 was created largely because of complaints from such provinces. Historians note that the system relied on annual amateur governors with wide discretion, a weakness that later produced figures like Verres. The 227 reform also coincides with the Ebro treaty and the Gallic danger, a period when Rome was consolidating its power in the west before the great war.

scholarship: Brennan, The Praetorship in the Roman Republic (2000)

set.detail:
In 226, alarmed by the build-up of a Gallic invasion in the Po valley and by the expansion of Hasdrubal's dominion in Spain, Rome sent envoys to Hasdrubal at New Carthage. Polybius (2.13, 3.27) says the agreement, made without referring to Carthage, bound the Carthaginians not to cross the river Iber under arms; nothing was said about the rest of Spain. Livy and Appian add that Saguntum, an Iberian city south of the river, was explicitly protected as an ally or that it was to be left free, but Polybius knows no such clause and says that Rome's friendship with Saguntum was separate and probably later than 226.

The treaty is central to the controversy over the origins of the Second Punic War. If the Iber is the Ebro, Saguntum (south of it) lay in the Carthaginian sphere and Hannibal's attack in 219 broke no treaty; Rome's case rested instead on its friendship with Saguntum, and its declaration of war would be aggression. Some scholars (Carcopino, and more recently others) have suggested that the Iber was a different river south of Saguntum, such as the Júcar, which would make the attack a breach; most reject this, because Polybius consistently locates the Iber north of Saguntum and Hannibal's crossing of the Iber is placed well north. Carthaginian spokesmen in 218 argued that the treaty was not binding, being made by Hasdrubal without ratification; the Romans replied, Polybius says, that the treaty of Lutatius protected allies and Saguntum was their ally.

Polybius regarded the Saguntine question as only the pretext (prophasis) and listed the true causes as Hamilcar's anger, the seizure of Sardinia and Carthaginian success in Spain. The Ebro treaty shows Rome trying to limit Carthaginian power in Spain cheaply while it dealt with the Gauls, an arrangement reflecting mutual recognition of spheres. Hasdrubal, for his part, gained Roman acceptance of the Carthaginian dominion up to the Ebro. The treaty held until Hannibal crossed the Ebro in spring 218, by which time the two states were already at war over Saguntum.

scholarship: Rich, The Origins of the Second Punic War, in Cornell, Rankov and Sabin (eds.), The Second Punic War: A Reappraisal (1996)
Sumner, Roman Policy in Spain before the Hannibalic War, HSCP 72 (1967)

set.detail:
Provoked by the Lex Flaminia's settlement of the ager Gallicus (232), the Boii and Insubres hired Gaesatae from beyond the Alps under the kings Concolitanus and Aneroestes and in 225 invaded Etruria. Polybius (2.23-31) gives their strength as 50,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry and chariots. Rome mobilised on an unprecedented scale (the manpower list of 225), stationing the praetor's army in Etruria, the consul Lucius Aemilius Papus at Ariminum, and calling the other consul, Gaius Atilius Regulus, back from Sardinia. The Gauls slipped past the Roman army in Etruria, reached Clusium, three days from Rome, and beat the praetor near Faesulae, but withdrew north along the coast when Papus came up, laden with plunder.

Regulus had landed at Pisae and was marching south along the Via Aurelia route when his scouts captured Gallic foragers near Telamon (Talamone). Learning that the Gauls were between him and Papus, he tried to seize a hill commanding the road with his cavalry and was killed; his head was brought to the Gallic kings. The Gauls formed a double front, Gaesatae and Insubres facing Papus to the rear, Taurisci and Boii facing Regulus' army ahead, with wagons and chariots on the wings. Polybius describes the naked Gaesatae in the front ranks, the gold torques and armlets, the din of trumpets, and the effect of Roman javelin men on unarmoured warriors. The Roman cavalry, winning on the hill, charged the Gallic flank and the infantry closed in from both sides.

Polybius reports 40,000 Gauls killed and 10,000 captured, including Concolitanus; Aneroestes killed himself. Papus ravaged the Boian country and triumphed, hanging standards and torques on the Capitol. The battle ended the last great Gallic invasion of peninsular Italy and led directly to the Roman offensive across the Po (224-222), the subjugation of the Insubres and the founding of Placentia and Cremona in 218. Polybius' detailed account, probably drawn from Fabius Pictor, an eyewitness, is one of the best descriptions of Celtic warfare. The site's location near Talamone is supported by a votive deposit of weapons found nearby and the Etruscan pediment of Talamonaccio.

scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)

set.detail:
Faced with the Gallic invasion of 225, Rome ordered its allies to send in lists of men capable of bearing arms, and Polybius (2.24) reproduces the results, probably from Fabius Pictor, who served in the campaign. The armies in the field included four consular legions of 5,200 foot and 300 horse each, with 30,000 allied foot and 2,000 horse; 50,000 foot and 4,000 horse of Sabines and Etruscans stationed in Etruria; 20,000 Umbrians and Sarsinates and 20,000 Veneti and Cenomani on the Boian frontier; and a reserve at Rome of 20,000 citizen foot and 1,500 horse with 30,000 allied foot and 2,000 horse.

The registers then listed those available: Latins 80,000 foot and 5,000 horse; Samnites 70,000 and 7,000; Iapygians and Messapians 50,000 and 16,000; Lucanians 30,000 and 3,000; Marsi, Marrucini, Frentani and Vestini 20,000 and 4,000; and Roman and Campanian citizens 250,000 foot and 23,000 horse. Polybius sums the total at over 700,000 foot and about 70,000 horse, and contrasts it with the 20,000 men with whom Hannibal entered Italy.

The list is the most important single document for the demography of Roman Italy and has been endlessly analysed. Brunt (Italian Manpower, 1971) argued that the figures include men up to 46 or older and that Polybius' totals contain errors of addition, such as omitting the Bruttians and Greeks; he estimated about 3 million free inhabitants of peninsular Italy, of whom about 900,000 were Roman citizens. Others (Lo Cascio, Scheidel) debate whether the census figures should be read as adult males or include others, which affects reconstructions of Italian population and of the Gracchan crisis. Baronowski argued that the figures reflect the formula togatorum, the system by which allied contingents were assessed. Whatever the precise reading, the list explains why Hannibal, despite three great victories, could not break Rome: the reservoir of manpower was larger than any Hellenistic kingdom could command, and it was organised.

scholarship: Baronowski, Roman Military Forces in 225 BC, Historia 42 (1993)
Lo Cascio, The Size of the Roman Population, JRS 84 (1994)

set.detail:
In 222 the consuls Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus continued the offensive against the Insubres, who had sued for peace and been rejected, and had recruited 30,000 Gaesatae. While Scipio besieged Acerrae, an Insubrian fortress on the Adda, the Insubres crossed the Po and besieged Clastidium (Casteggio), a town of the Anares allied to Rome, to draw the Romans off. Marcellus rode to its relief with the cavalry and some light infantry.

Polybius (2.34) says only that the Roman cavalry charged and routed the Gauls at Clastidium. Plutarch (Marcellus 6-8), following a richer tradition, has Marcellus single out the Gallic king Viridomarus (Britomartus in some texts), who had challenged him, and kill him in single combat on horseback, after vowing the finest armour to Jupiter Feretrius. Marcellus stripped the body and dedicated the spolia opima on the Capitol, only the third Roman in history, after Romulus and Aulus Cornelius Cossus, to do so; he rode in his triumph holding a tree trunk hung with the king's armour. Naevius wrote a historical play, Clastidium, on the victory, possibly for the funeral games of Marcellus in 208 or the dedication of the temple of Honos and Virtus in 205.

After Clastidium Scipio took Acerrae and Mediolanum, and the Insubres surrendered. The battle and the spolia opima laid the foundation of Marcellus' fame and of his family's claim to Sicilian and Gallic patronage. Historians accept the victory but treat the duel with caution, since spolia opima stories were embellished by family tradition; Augustus later used the question of who was entitled to the honour against Marcus Licinius Crassus in 27 BC. Marcellus vowed a temple to Honos and Virtus, dedicated by his son in 205. The conquest of the Insubres proved short-lived: four years later, Hannibal's arrival brought them back into arms.

scholarship: Flower, The Tradition of the Spolia Opima, ClAnt 19 (2000)
Rich, Augustus and the Spolia Opima, Chiron 26 (1996)

set.detail:
Hasdrubal, son-in-law of Hamilcar, commanded in Spain from 229 to 221, elected by the army and confirmed by the Carthaginian people. He expanded Carthaginian rule by diplomacy as much as by war: he married the daughter of an Iberian king and was acclaimed supreme general (strategos autokrator) by the Iberians, according to Diodorus; he founded New Carthage (Qart Hadasht) on a great natural harbour around 227 and built a palace there, which Polybius heard criticised as a sign of royal ambitions; and he made the Ebro treaty with Rome in 226. Polybius (2.36) says that his army numbered 50,000 foot, 6,000 horse and 200 elephants.

In 221 he was murdered at night in his quarters at New Carthage by a Celt with a private grudge. Livy (21.2) says the killer was a slave avenging his master whom Hasdrubal had executed, and that the man smiled under torture; Appian adds that he was a slave of an Iberian noble. The army immediately acclaimed the 25-year-old Hannibal, Hamilcar's son, who had served under Hasdrubal, as commander, and the Carthaginian assembly ratified the choice.

Fabius Pictor, quoted by Polybius (3.8), claimed that Hasdrubal had tried to seize power at Carthage and, failing, ruled Spain independently, and that the Second War was caused by his ambition and that of the Barcid faction. Polybius rejects this argument because the Carthaginian government endorsed Hannibal's actions. Modern historians debate the Barcid 'monarchy' in Spain, pointing to the portrait coinage of Carthago Nova and the dynasty's marriage alliances, as evidence of a quasi-Hellenistic regime that remained nonetheless dependent on Carthage (Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty). The murder changed the course of history: Hasdrubal had a reputation for prudence and diplomacy, and his young successor turned at once to military campaigns against the Olcades and Vaccaei, and then against Saguntum.

Saguntum (Sagunto), an Iberian town on a rocky ridge a few kilometres from the coast, about 140 kilometres south of the Ebro, had entered into friendship with Rome some years before 219, perhaps in the 230s or after the Ebro treaty; Polybius says the Saguntines had chosen Rome as arbiter in a civic dispute and that Rome had executed some leading men of the pro-Carthaginian faction. Hannibal, using a quarrel between Saguntum and its neighbours the Torboletae (or Turdetani) as a pretext, laid siege in spring 219. Roman envoys came to him in his winter quarters in 220/19 and to Carthage, warning him to leave Saguntum alone; he replied that Rome had acted unjustly in Saguntum.

The siege lasted eight months. Livy's account (21.6-15) is full of drama: Hannibal was wounded in the thigh by a javelin, the defenders used the falarica, a fire-javelin with a long iron head, and the citizens, at the end, threw their gold and silver into a fire and many chose death. When the city fell, Hannibal killed the adult males, enslaved the rest and sent the booty to Carthage and to the army, ensuring support for war. Rome, preoccupied with the Second Illyrian War, sent no help.

The Roman tradition made the siege the outrage that justified war, but Polybius (3.6-33) distinguishes pretext from cause and examines the legal case: the Carthaginians argued that Saguntum lay outside the Ebro treaty's area and that the treaty itself was invalid, while Rome relied on its friendship with Saguntum. Modern opinion is that Hannibal's attack did not breach a formal treaty, but that he knew it would mean war, and that Rome's eight months of inaction reflect either indecision or an expectation that the war would be fought in Spain and Africa. The Saguntines became a symbol of fides; Rome restored the city after recapturing it, and Saguntum later struck coins and became a municipium. Remains of the Iberian and Roman town survive on the hill.

scholarship: Rich, The Origins of the Second Punic War, in Cornell et al. (eds.), The Second Punic War: A Reappraisal (1996)

set.detail:
After news of Saguntum's fall reached Rome early in 218, an embassy was sent to Carthage. Polybius (3.20, 3.33) names no leader; Livy (21.18) names Quintus Fabius, usually taken as Quintus Fabius Maximus, though some think of Marcus Fabius Buteo. The envoys demanded that Carthage surrender Hannibal and his council for punishment or face war. In the Carthaginian senate, speakers argued that Saguntum was not covered by the Lutatius treaty, which only protected the allies of each party at the time, and that the Ebro treaty, made by Hasdrubal without ratification, did not bind Carthage. The Romans replied that the question was not one of argument but of Roman honour.

Fabius then gathered his toga into a fold and said that he held there both peace and war: they could take whichever they liked. The suffete told him to give whichever he chose; when he said war, the Carthaginian senators shouted that they accepted it. Polybius and Livy record this scene; Dio and Zonaras have a different version with a debate in the Roman Senate, in which Lucius Cornelius Lentulus urged war and Quintus Fabius caution. The comitia centuriata voted the declaration, and the legal ritual of the fetiales may have been adapted for an overseas enemy.

The Roman war plan was offensive: the consul Tiberius Sempronius Longus with two legions and 160 quinqueremes was to cross to Sicily and then to Africa, and Publius Cornelius Scipio was to go to Spain with two legions and 60 ships. The plan assumed that Rome controlled the sea and that the war would be fought abroad. Hannibal upset it by marching overland to Italy. Historians debate whether Rome deliberately provoked the war, assuming an easy victory, or acted out of genuine fear of Carthaginian power in Spain. Polybius thought the war inevitable given Carthaginian resentment; the dramatic scene in the Carthaginian senate became a set piece of Roman memory, depicting a Rome that chose war openly in the name of fides.

scholarship: Rich, Declaring War in the Roman Republic (1976)

set.detail:
Shortly before the war, the tribune Quintus Claudius carried a plebiscite forbidding senators and their sons to own a seagoing ship with a capacity of more than 300 amphorae, which Livy (21.63) says was considered enough to transport produce from their estates; all profit-seeking (quaestus omnis) was thought unworthy of senators. Gaius Flaminius alone among the senators supported the law, which won him great popularity with the people and hatred in the Senate; Livy links this with his second consulship (217) and his disregard for the ceremonies of entering office.

The law probably did not eliminate senatorial trade but forced it into indirect forms: senators lent money for maritime ventures through freedmen and agents, as Cato did through his freedman Quintio, and invested in land, which became the respectable form of senatorial wealth. Cicero mentions the law (Verrines 2.5.45) as still in force, although obsolete in practice, and Caesar's lex Iulia de repetundis of 59 renewed similar provisions. The law also had the effect of defining a separate class of wealthy non-senators engaged in trade and public contracts, the future equestrian order, whose interests would diverge from those of the Senate.

Modern interpretations differ. Some see it as an attempt by Flaminius and his supporters to prevent senators from competing unfairly with the traders and contractors who had been the beneficiaries of the war economy; others (Yavetz, D'Arms) see it as an expression of aristocratic ideology, reinforcing an ethos of land-based wealth and ensuring that senators would not be distracted by commerce. The capacity of 300 amphorae, about 7 to 8 tonnes, suggests that small coastal vessels transporting the produce of the senator's own estates were permitted. The law is often cited in discussions of the 'primitivist' versus 'modernist' debate about the Roman economy.

scholarship: D'Arms, Commerce and Social Standing in Ancient Rome (1981)
Yavetz, The Policy of Gaius Flaminius and the Plebiscitum Claudianum, Athenaeum 40 (1962)

set.detail:
Hannibal left New Carthage in late spring 218 with, Polybius says, 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse, crossed the Ebro, fought his way through the Ilergetes and other tribes of Catalonia, left Hanno with 11,000 men to hold the area, crossed the Pyrenees and reached the Rhône in about late August. After forcing the crossing against the Volcae and evading Publius Scipio, who arrived at the Rhône three days too late, he marched upstream to the 'Island', where he settled a dispute between two Allobrogian brothers and received supplies. In October he entered the Alps.

Polybius, who claims to have walked the route himself and interviewed survivors, gives a 15-day crossing. On the ascent, the Allobroges ambushed the column in a defile; Hannibal occupied the heights by night and drove them off, taking a town. Later, mountain people who had offered guides and hostages attacked the column in a gorge, and Hannibal spent a night separated from his cavalry and baggage near a 'white rock'. On the ninth day he reached the summit, where he camped two days and showed his men the plains of Italy. The descent was the hardest part: a landslide had carried away the path, and snow had fallen; Livy (21.37) says Hannibal split the rocks with fire and vinegar. The army arrived in the territory of the Taurini with 20,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry, according to Hannibal's own inscription at Lacinium.

The pass remains a matter of debate: the Col du Clapier, Mont Cenis, the Little St Bernard, the Col de Montgenèvre and the Col de la Traversette all have advocates. In 2016 Mahaney and colleagues reported a disturbed layer of horse dung dated to about the right period near the Col de la Traversette, a finding still disputed. The elephants, 37 at the outset, survived the crossing but most died after the Trebia. The march became the defining legend of Hannibal, but its strategic purpose was clear: to bring the war to Italy, raise the Gauls, and break Rome's alliance system.

scholarship: Mahaney et al., Biostratigraphic evidence relating to the age-old question of Hannibal's invasion of Italy, Archaeometry 59 (2017)

set.detail:
After the Ticinus, Publius Scipio, wounded, withdrew across the Po to the Trebia, a tributary south of the Po near Placentia, and waited for his colleague Tiberius Sempronius Longus, recalled from Sicily, who marched his army to Ariminum in forty days. The two consular armies, about 36,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry, camped together on the east bank. Hannibal had about 28,000 infantry, 10,000 cavalry and his elephants, and the support of the Boii and Insubres.

Sempronius, eager for battle before his term ended and before Scipio could recover, was encouraged by a cavalry success. On a snowy day around the winter solstice (Polybius 3.72), Hannibal sent the Numidians across the river to provoke the Romans at dawn, and Sempronius sent his whole army, unfed, across the icy river, swollen with rain, in pursuit. Meanwhile Hannibal's brother Mago had hidden in a watercourse with 1,000 cavalry and 1,000 infantry the night before. The Roman infantry crossed chest-deep and formed on the west bank, cold and hungry, facing Hannibal's fresh army. The Carthaginian cavalry and elephants drove off the Roman cavalry on the wings, and Mago fell on the Roman rear.

The Roman centre, about 10,000 men, broke through the Carthaginian line and marched to Placentia in good order; the rest of the army was trapped against the river and destroyed. Polybius does not give total Roman losses; modern estimates are 20,000 to 30,000. Hannibal's losses were mainly among the Gauls; most of his elephants died in the cold. Sempronius reported that the weather had denied him victory. The battle, in which Hannibal used terrain, ambush and fresh troops against an impetuous commander, foreshadowed Trasimene and Cannae, and brought the Gauls of the Po valley over to him in large numbers. Rome's Cisalpine colonies at Placentia and Cremona held out, and the debate about how to fight Hannibal began in earnest.

In spring 217 Hannibal crossed the Apennines and marched through the marshes of the Arno, where he lost an eye to infection, and devastated Etruria to provoke the consul Gaius Flaminius, who was at Arretium with about 25,000 men. Flaminius, a popular hero who had defied the Senate and entered his consulship without the usual ceremonies, pursued him. On the morning of 21 June 217 by the Roman calendar (Ovid's date) Hannibal waited on the hills above the narrow road along the north shore of Lake Trasimene, near modern Tuoro sul Trasimeno.

The Roman column entered the defile in a morning mist. Hannibal had deployed his African and Spanish infantry on a hill at the far end, his light troops and Gauls in the hills along the side, and his cavalry at the entrance. At his signal the whole army charged down. The Romans, caught in marching order, had no time to form a line. Flaminius was killed by an Insubrian horseman named Ducarius, according to Livy. About 15,000 Romans died, many drowning in the lake; 6,000 broke through at the front and were captured the next day by Maharbal; about 10,000 escaped to Rome. Hannibal lost about 1,500, mostly Gauls. Livy says that an earthquake that destroyed cities in Italy went unnoticed by the combatants.

The defeat was the largest ambush in Roman military history. The praetor Marcus Pomponius announced 'we have been defeated in a great battle' to the people in the Forum. A few days later Centenius' 4,000 cavalry were destroyed. The disaster led to the dictatorship of Fabius and the religious measures of 217. Flaminius was blamed by the senatorial tradition (Fabius Pictor) for impiety and recklessness, but some modern scholars think he was trying to keep Hannibal under observation and was tricked by superior intelligence. The precise battlefield is debated: older theories placed it in the narrow pass near Passignano; more recent studies of the lake's ancient shoreline, which was further north, favour the Tuoro plain; cremation pits found there have been associated with the dead, though this is disputed.

scholarship: Gilliver, Battle of Lake Trasimene, in Hoyos (ed.) (2011)

set.detail:
After Trasimene, with one consul dead and the other, Gnaeus Servilius Geminus, cut off from Rome, the people elected Quintus Fabius Maximus dictator (Livy says prodictator, since only a consul could legally appoint a dictator) and Marcus Minucius Rufus his master of horse. Fabius began with religious measures, then took command of four legions and, avoiding pitched battle, followed Hannibal through Apulia and Campania, keeping to high ground, cutting off foragers and harassing his supply. This strategy of delay earned him first the insult Paedagogus (Hannibal's tutor) and later the honourable cognomen Cunctator.

Hannibal ravaged the Ager Falernus, one of the richest areas of Italy, to provoke Fabius and the Campanian allies. Fabius blocked the passes, but Hannibal escaped by night by driving 2,000 oxen with burning torches on their horns up a hill, distracting the Roman guard. Fabius' strategy was unpopular: his estate was spared by Hannibal, raising suspicions. While Fabius was in Rome for religious duties, Minucius won a skirmish near Gerunium, and the people passed the Lex Metilia giving him equal command, an unprecedented measure. Minucius divided the army, was trapped by Hannibal, and saved by Fabius; he then returned to subordination, calling Fabius his father.

Ennius' line, 'unus homo nobis cunctando restituit rem' ('one man by delaying restored the state'), immortalised Fabius. Polybius (3.89-90) explains the logic: Hannibal was in hostile territory, without a secure base, while Rome had inexhaustible manpower; time was on Rome's side if it avoided disaster. After the dictatorship expired, the consuls of 216 abandoned the strategy for a decisive battle, and the result was Cannae, after which the Fabian strategy was adopted for the rest of the war. Modern assessments note that Fabius' strategy was not purely passive: it included sieges, attacks on Hannibal's allies, and attempts to wear down his army; and that his political enemies, especially popular figures like Varro, criticised it for allowing the devastation of allied land.

scholarship: Erdkamp, Polybius, Livy and the Fabian Strategy, AncSoc 23 (1992)

set.detail:
The Fourth Syrian War (219-217) saw Antiochus III, then 24, attempt to reconquer Coele-Syria, which the Ptolemies had held since 301. After seizing Seleucia in Pieria, Tyre and Ptolemais by the treachery of the Ptolemaic general Theodotus, Antiochus marched south in 217 with, Polybius says (5.79), 62,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and 102 Indian elephants. Ptolemy IV, whose ministers Sosibius and Agathocles had spent two years training a new army, met him near Raphia, south of Gaza, with 70,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry and 73 African elephants. The army included, for the first time, 20,000 native Egyptians trained and armed as a Macedonian phalanx.

On 22 June 217 the armies fought. Antiochus, commanding his right, routed the Ptolemaic left; his Indian elephants drove off the smaller African forest elephants, which, Polybius says, could not stand the smell and the trumpeting of the Indian animals. But Antiochus pursued too far. In the centre, the Ptolemaic phalanx, with the Egyptians, broke the Seleucid phalanx; Ptolemy, who had joined the centre, was decisive. The Seleucids lost about 10,000 infantry and 300 cavalry killed and 4,000 captured; the Ptolemies 1,500 infantry and 700 cavalry. Antiochus withdrew and made peace, giving up Coele-Syria.

Polybius' account (5.79-86) is one of the most detailed of any Hellenistic battle, and is complemented by the Raphia Decree, a trilingual (Greek, hieroglyphic, demotic) inscription set up by the Egyptian priests at Memphis to honour Ptolemy. Polybius notes that the arming of Egyptians had long-term consequences: emboldened by their victory, they revolted in the following decades, notably in the great revolt of the Thebaid (205-186). The battle came at the same moment as Trasimene, and Polybius uses this coincidence (the 'symploke' or interweaving of events) to begin his account of the growing unity of Mediterranean history. Antiochus rebuilt his power in his eastern anabasis and returned to win Coele-Syria at Panium in 200.

The Social War of 220-217 pitted Philip V and the Hellenic alliance founded by Antigonus Doson, including the Achaeans, against the Aetolians, Spartans and Eleans. Philip, aged 17 to 21, won a series of brilliant victories, including the sack of the Aetolian federal sanctuary at Thermum (218). In summer 217, when news of Trasimene arrived, Philip, on the advice of Demetrius of Pharos, who wanted to recover his Illyrian possessions, decided to make peace and turn west.

At the peace conference at Naupactus, which recognised the status quo, Polybius (5.104) gives the Aetolian Agelaus a famous speech: the Greeks should unite and stop fighting among themselves, because whoever won the great war in Italy, Rome or Carthage, would not be content with the West but would extend their power to Greece. He urged Philip to watch the 'clouds rising in the west' and warned that otherwise the Greeks would no longer be able to make war or peace at their own will. The speech is generally regarded as a composition by Polybius, perhaps based on a real speech, illustrating his thesis that the year 217 marked the beginning of the interweaving of the history of the Mediterranean world.

The peace of Naupactus closed the Social War on favourable terms for Macedon, which kept its gains. Philip then built a fleet of 100 lembi in winter 217/16, sailed into the Adriatic in 216, and fled when he heard of the approach of a small Roman squadron, a humiliating start. After Cannae, he allied with Hannibal (215). Modern historians (Walbank, Eckstein) see Naupactus as a turning point in Polybius' narrative structure and in Macedonian policy, while noting that Philip's aims were limited: the recovery of Illyria, not the conquest of Italy. The Roman response, the First Macedonian War, was waged largely through allies like the Aetolians, the very people Agelaus had warned.

scholarship: Champion, Cultural Politics in Polybius's Histories (2004)

set.detail:
In 216 Rome abandoned the Fabian strategy and raised eight legions, the largest army it had ever fielded, under the consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro, with the proconsuls Gnaeus Servilius Geminus and Marcus Atilius Regulus. Polybius (3.107-117) gives 80,000 infantry and over 6,000 cavalry; Livy records conflicting figures. Hannibal had seized the Roman supply depot at Cannae on the Aufidus (Ofanto) in Apulia, with about 40,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry. On 2 August (Roman calendar), Varro, who held command that day under the alternating system, deployed on the right bank of the river with the infantry in deeper and narrower formations than usual, hoping to break the Carthaginian centre by weight.

Hannibal advanced his Gallic and Spanish infantry in a crescent bulging towards the Romans, with his African veterans in deep columns on each flank. Hasdrubal's heavy cavalry on the left destroyed the Roman cavalry along the river, then rode behind the Roman army to help the Numidians rout the allied cavalry on the other wing. The Roman infantry pushed the crescent back until it was concave; the Africans then turned inwards and attacked the Roman flanks, and Hasdrubal's cavalry attacked the rear. The Romans were surrounded and massacred.

Polybius says 70,000 Romans were killed and 10,000 captured; Livy gives 48,200 killed and 19,300 captured. Paullus, Servilius, Minucius Rufus, 80 senators and 29 military tribunes died. Hannibal lost about 5,700, mostly Gauls. Varro escaped with 70 horsemen to Venusia; the Senate thanked him for not despairing of the Republic. Livy has Maharbal tell Hannibal 'you know how to win a victory, but not how to use it', after he refused to march on Rome. Cannae became the model of the double envelopment, studied by Schlieffen and generations of staff colleges. Modern debate centres on the site (right or left bank of the Ofanto), on the numbers, and on the reasons for Roman tactics. Its political result was the defection of much of southern Italy, including Capua, but the Latin colonies and central Italy held firm.

scholarship: Daly, Cannae: The Experience of Battle in the Second Punic War (2002)
Samuels, The Reality of Cannae, MGM 47 (1990)

set.detail:
The news of Cannae, Livy (22.54-61) says, caused unprecedented panic in Rome, with mourning in every house; the Senate, on Fabius' advice, posted guards at the gates, forbade women to mourn in public, and limited mourning to thirty days so that the rites of Ceres could be performed. Quintus Fabius Pictor was sent to Delphi to ask how to appease the gods. Two Vestals, Opimia and Floronia, were convicted of unchastity: one was buried alive at the Colline Gate, the other committed suicide. On the instruction of the Sibylline Books, a Gallic man and woman and a Greek man and woman were buried alive in the Forum Boarium, an act Livy calls 'hardly Roman'.

Militarily, Rome showed extraordinary resilience. Marcus Junius Pera was named dictator; he raised four new legions, enrolled youths of 17 and under, and bought and armed 8,000 slaves (the volones), who were promised freedom for valour; 6,000 debtors and criminals were released and armed. Weapons were taken from the temples, including trophies from earlier wars. The Senate refused to ransom the 8,000 prisoners held by Hannibal, and sent the survivors of Cannae to serve in Sicily without discharge. Marcus Fabius Buteo was appointed a second dictator to refill the Senate. New taxes were imposed; the bankers' board of triumviri mensarii was created.

Polybius (3.118, 6.58) saw Rome's response to Cannae as proof of the excellence of its constitution, the reason why it recovered and conquered the world in 53 years. Modern historians emphasise the role of the alliance system: although Capua, much of Samnium, Apulia, Lucania and Bruttium defected, the Latin colonies and the communities of central Italy remained loyal, giving Rome a manpower reserve Hannibal could not match. The human sacrifice of 216, and of 228 and probably 114/113, remains among the most discussed features of Republican religion; Livy's discomfort shows that it was felt as un-Roman even at the time.

scholarship: Beard, North and Price, Religions of Rome (1998)

set.detail:
Capua, the largest city of Campania and, with perhaps 30,000 fighting men, the second most powerful community of Roman Italy, had held a special status since 338: its people were Roman citizens without the vote (cives sine suffragio), and its aristocracy had intermarried with the Roman nobility. After Cannae, the Capuan popular leader Pacuvius Calavius, who had married a daughter of Appius Claudius, and the meddix Vibius Virrius led the city to Hannibal. Livy says the Capuans first sent an embassy to Varro and heard of the scale of the disaster, then negotiated with Hannibal.

The terms, according to Livy (23.7), were that no Carthaginian general or magistrate should have authority over a Campanian citizen, that no Campanian should be forced to serve in war or perform any duty against his will, that Capua should keep its laws and magistrates, and that Hannibal should hand over 300 Roman prisoners for exchange with the Campanian cavalrymen serving in Sicily. Livy adds that the Capuans hoped to become the leading city of Italy after Rome's defeat. Roman citizens in Capua were shut in the baths and suffocated. Decius Magius, the leader of the pro-Roman faction, was arrested and sent to Carthage, but his ship was driven to Cyrene, where he took refuge with Ptolemy.

Capua's defection, followed by Atella, Calatia, some of the Hirpini and Samnites, was Hannibal's greatest political success, but it proved a liability: Capua became a fixed point he had to defend, and Roman armies gradually tightened their grip. The siege of 212-211 and the city's fall, with the execution of its senate and the confiscation of its territory, were Rome's most terrible revenge. Livy's account is coloured by moralising about Capuan luxury, the 'delights of Capua' that supposedly softened Hannibal's army in winter 216/15, a story most historians reject. Modern studies (Fronda) explain Capua's choice through local rivalries and its ambitions in Campania, rather than simple luxury or ingratitude.

scholarship: Fronda, Between Rome and Carthage: Southern Italy during the Second Punic War (2010)

set.detail:
In 215 Philip V sent the Athenian Xenophanes as envoy to Hannibal in Italy. On his way back the envoy was captured by a Roman ship off Calabria with the Carthaginian envoys and the text of the agreement; the Romans learned of the alliance and sent a fleet to Brundisium under the praetor Marcus Valerius Laevinus. Polybius (7.9) preserves the Greek text of the oath sworn by Hannibal, Mago, Myrcan and Barmocar, and the members of the Carthaginian council present, before the gods of Carthage, the Greek gods and the gods of the army.

The treaty provided that Philip and Hannibal would be allies against Rome; that the Carthaginians would protect Philip and the Macedonians, and Philip the Carthaginians; that when the gods gave them victory, Rome would be bound not to make war on Philip or to control Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus, Pharos, Dimale, the Parthini and Atintania, and that Demetrius of Pharos would recover his possessions. Nothing is said about Philip invading Italy. Livy (23.33) has a different version in which Philip was to land in Italy with 200 ships, and Italy would go to Carthage and Greece to Macedon after the war; this is probably a Roman fabrication or misunderstanding.

The text, with its Punic religious formulas translated into Greek (the 'daimon of the Carthaginians', Heracles, Iolaos), is of great interest for the study of Carthaginian religion and diplomatic practice, and has been analysed by Bickerman and Barré. It shows that Hannibal envisaged a negotiated peace in which Rome survived but was diminished, rather than the destruction of Rome. The treaty led directly to the First Macedonian War, which Rome conducted with few forces, relying on the Aetolian League and later Attalus I. Its strategic effect was minimal, since Philip never sent troops to Italy, but the memory of his alliance with Hannibal shaped Roman attitudes towards Macedon and contributed to the war of 200.

scholarship: Bickerman, An Oath of Hannibal, TAPhA 75 (1944)
Barré, The God-List in the Treaty between Hannibal and Philip V of Macedonia (1983)

set.detail:
In 215 Carthage ordered Hasdrubal Barca to march to Italy to reinforce his brother. The Scipio brothers, Gnaeus and Publius, who had established a base north of the Ebro at Tarraco since 218 and had won at Cissa and in the naval battle of the Ebro mouth, crossed the Ebro and besieged Ibera, the main town near the mouth, to force a battle. Hasdrubal attacked and the armies met near Ibera (perhaps near Dertosa, modern Tortosa) in spring or summer 215. Livy (23.28-29) is the only detailed source.

The two armies were roughly equal, about 25,000 each. Hasdrubal placed his Spanish infantry in the centre, with Africans and Carthaginians on the flanks and cavalry on the wings, a formation similar to Cannae. But the Spaniards in the centre, unwilling to fight so far from home, broke at once before the Roman legions, and the Romans then turned on the African flanks. The Carthaginian cavalry fled as soon as it saw the centre break. Hasdrubal escaped with a few men; his camp was taken.

The battle had enormous strategic consequences. It kept Hasdrubal in Spain for seven years, prevented reinforcements from reaching Hannibal in the critical period after Cannae, and caused several Spanish peoples to go over to Rome. Carthage diverted to Spain the army of Mago, which had been intended for Italy. Modern historians (Lazenby) consider Dertosa one of the decisive battles of the war, although less celebrated than the Italian battles. The Scipios then pushed south, recapturing Saguntum (212) and recruiting Celtiberian mercenaries. However, Livy's account of the Spanish war in this period is unreliable, mixing real battles with others probably invented or inflated by later annalists, and the date and location of Dertosa have also been questioned.

When Syracuse went over to Carthage in 214, after the murder of Hieronymus and the rise of Hippocrates and Epicydes, Marcellus and Appius Claudius Pulcher besieged it by land and sea in 213. The city, whose walls Dionysius I had extended to enclose the plateau of Epipolae and the fortress of Euryalus, was one of the largest and best defended in the Mediterranean. Polybius (8.3-7), Livy and Plutarch describe the role of Archimedes, then about 75. His catapults, graded to hit ships at long and short range, his small scorpions shooting through slits in the walls, and his cranes ('iron hands') that lifted the bows of Roman ships and dropped them, defeated Marcellus' assault from the sea, including a sambuca, a scaling ladder mounted on eight quinqueremes lashed together.

The Romans settled for a blockade. In spring 212, during the festival of Artemis, when the defenders had been drinking, a Roman party scaled the wall near the Hexapylon at a point where Marcellus had calculated the wall's height by counting stones during a parley. Marcellus took Epipolae and the outer quarters of Tyche and Neapolis; Euryalus surrendered. The Carthaginian army of Himilco and Hippocrates, camped outside, was destroyed by plague in the autumn. Achradina and Ortygia held out until a Spanish officer, Moericus, betrayed part of Ortygia. The city was sacked; Archimedes was killed.

Marcellus carried off to Rome a vast quantity of statues and paintings, which Livy and Polybius identify as the beginning of Roman enthusiasm for Greek art and the decline of Roman austerity. Polybius (9.10) warns that taking the art of the conquered breeds envy and that Rome should not have imitated them. The story of Archimedes burning the Roman ships with mirrors is a later invention (Lucian, Galen, then Byzantine authors). The fall of Syracuse ended Hiero's kingdom; Syracuse became the capital of the province of Sicily, and the Syracusans complained to the Senate in 210 about Marcellus' conduct. The siege is one of the classic examples of ancient siege warfare and of Greek science applied to war.

After Hannibal's capture of Tarentum in 212, Rome concentrated on Capua. The consuls Quintus Fulvius Flaccus and Appius Claudius Pulcher, reinforced in 211 by the praetor Gaius Claudius Nero, surrounded the city with a double line of ditch and rampart, one facing the city and one facing outwards. With about 60,000 men, they starved the city while Hannibal was in the south. Hannibal returned in 211 and attacked the lines while the Capuans sallied, but failed to break through, and then made his famous march on Rome, hoping to draw the besiegers away. Fulvius detached only a part of his army to defend Rome, and the siege continued.

When Hannibal withdrew south, Capua surrendered. Livy (26.12-16) says that Vibius Virrius and 27 senators chose to die at a banquet, drinking poison. Fulvius had 53 Capuan senators beheaded, 28 at Cales and 25 at Teanum, reportedly before he opened a letter from the Senate recommending clemency, which he held in his hand. The remaining citizens were sold or moved; the city lost its civic institutions, its magistrates and its assembly; its territory, the rich Ager Campanus, was confiscated and leased by the censors, providing a valuable income for the Roman state for over a century. Capua became a market town administered by a prefect sent from Rome.

The fall of Capua was a turning point in the war. It showed Rome's allies in southern Italy that Hannibal could not protect them, and many began to return. Livy's account emphasises Roman severity and the justice of punishing Capuan treachery. The legend of Capuan luxury and the 'delights of Capua' supposedly corrupting Hannibal's army is generally rejected. The Ager Campanus remained public land until Caesar distributed it in 59. Modern historians stress the military skill of the double-line siege, a technique Caesar would later use at Alesia, and the political lesson: Rome's treatment of Capua deterred further defections.
